shortSummary: Aromatic golden-orange Asteraceae annual prized for festive garlands, lutein carotenoids, and nematode-suppressing roots.
leadOverview: African or Aztec marigold (Tagetes erecta) is a vigorous, sun-loving annual renowned for dense pompom flower heads glowing in shades of saffron, amber, and lemon yellow. Native to Mexico and Central America, marigold has become deeply woven into South Asian festivals, companion gardening, and natural carotenoid production.

sections.title: Morphological Description
sections.subtitle: Pinnately divided aromatic leaves, oil glands, and globular capitula
sections.summary: Anatomy of deeply lobed foliage, fluted hollow peduncles, and dense ray-floret heads.
paragraphs: Tagetes erecta grows as an upright, ribbed herbaceous annual reaching 30 to 110 centimetres high with sturdy hollow-stemmed branches. Its pinnately compound leaves consist of 11 to 17 narrow, sharply toothed lanceolate leaflets dotted with translucent marginal oil glands that release a pungent, herbaceous-citrus scent when bruised.

Each terminal flower head sits atop a swollen, fluted peduncle and is enclosed by a fused cylindrical cup of green involucral bracts. Cultivated forms exhibit dozens of overlapping ruffled ray florets creating globular blooms 6 to 12 centimetres wide, maturing into slender black linear achenes topped with bristly pappus scales.

subblocks.heading: Ribbed Stems
subblocks.text: Erect angular green stems branching freely from middle nodes and swelling beneath each terminal flower bud.

subblocks.heading: Pinnate Foliage
subblocks.text: Dark green fern-like leaves bearing embedded pellucid oil glands secreting defensive thiophenes and tagetone.

subblocks.heading: Globular Capitula
subblocks.text: Dense double-rayed composite heads ranging from pale cream-gold to deep burnt tangerine.

subblocks.heading: Fibrous Roots
subblocks.text: Dense shallow fibrous root mat exuding allelopathic alpha-terthienyl into surrounding rhizosphere soil.

sections.title: Taxonomy & Botanical Classification
sections.subtitle: Tagetes vs Calendula clarification
sections.summary: Distinguishing New World Tagetes (Asteraceae) from Old World pot marigold (Calendula).
paragraphs: Tagetes erecta belongs to tribe Tageteae within family Asteraceae—a New World lineage characterized by aromatic oil glands on leaves and fused single-row involucral bracts. Despite its misleading common name 'African marigold', the species originated entirely in Mesoamerica before Spanish galleons dispersed it globally in the sixteenth century.
Botanists carefully distinguish Tagetes from Mediterranean pot marigold (Calendula officinalis), which belongs to a separate tribe and lacks pungent thiophene glands.

sections.title: Natural Habitat & Global Distribution
sections.subtitle: Mexican highlands to South Asian winter floriculture
sections.summary: Warm open slopes and commercial production across Jashore and Gazipur.
paragraphs: Wild ancestors of Tagetes erecta inhabit sunny disturbed slopes, open pine-oak clearings, and agricultural margins across Mexico and Guatemala between 800 and 2,300 metres altitude. Rapid maturation (55–70 days from seed to flower) allowed effortless naturalization across tropical and temperate continents.

In Bangladesh and India, marigold ('Genda') ranks among the highest-volume winter and spring flowers, extensively farmed in Jashore, Savar, and West Bengal for civic celebrations, weddings, and religious offerings.

sections.title: Ecological Role & Pollinator Interactions
sections.subtitle: Soil nematode suppression and hoverfly attraction
sections.summary: Allelopathic alpha-terthienyl against root-knot nematodes and beneficial insect recruitment.
paragraphs: Marigolds play a celebrated agroecological role in integrated pest management. Their roots synthesize and release alpha-terthienyl—a potent sulfur-containing compound activated by peroxidase enzymes—which disrupts cell membranes of destructive root-knot nematodes (Meloidogyne spp.) when intercropped with tomatoes, brinjal, or chillies.

Above ground, open single and semi-double flowers supply pollen and nectar to hoverflies (Syrphidae), ladybird beetles, and parasitic wasps that prey on aphids, while strong leaf volatiles partially mask host-plant scents from whiteflies.

sections.title: Economic, Culinary & Cultural Importance
sections.subtitle: Cempasúchil, South Asian garlands, and natural lutein dye
sections.summary: Ceremonial flower chains, textile dyeing, and macular carotenoid industry.
paragraphs: Known as Cempasúchil in Mexico, Tagetes erecta illuminates Día de los Muertos altars with golden petal paths, while across Bangladesh and India it forms thick, resilient garlands for Ekushey February, Pohela Boishakh, Durga Puja, and weddings.

Industrially, dried marigold petals represent the premier botanical source of natural lutein and zeaxanthin—extracted worldwide for food colouring, textile dyeing, and poultry feed to deepen egg-yolk pigmentation.

sections.title: Traditional & Scientific Medicinal Properties
sections.subtitle: Ocular lutein bioavailability and traditional topical pastes
sections.summary: Macular pigment protection and folk antimicrobial leaf poultices.
paragraphs: Modern nutritional science prizes purified Tagetes erecta petal extracts for standardized lutein and zeaxanthin—carotenoids that selectively accumulate in the human retinal macula, filtering high-energy blue light and supporting long-term visual acuity in age-related macular research.

In South Asian folk practice, fresh crushed marigold leaves are applied externally as an antiseptic poultice on minor cuts to staunch bleeding, while mild petal infusions have been studied for antioxidant phenolic activity.
sections.safetyNote: Do not confuse culinary Calendula officinalis with Tagetes erecta for heavy internal herbal teas; Tagetes essential oils contain potent ketones (tagetone) and phototoxic thiophenes that may cause contact dermatitis or uterine stimulation if taken in concentrated doses.

sections.title: Comprehensive Cultivation & Care Guide
sections.subtitle: Pinching, well-drained beds, and spider-mite vigilance
sections.summary: Full-sun planting, moderate watering at soil level, and deadheading.
paragraphs: Sow marigold seeds shallowly in warm, friable soil (pH 6.0–7.0) receiving at least 6 to 8 hours of direct sunlight; germination occurs rapidly within 5 to 7 days. Avoid excessive nitrogen fertilizer, which stimulates lush leafy stems at the expense of flower bud density.

Pinch terminal shoots when seedlings reach 15 centimetres to encourage compact, multi-stemmed crowns, and water at the root zone in the morning so dense double flower heads do not trap moisture and develop Botrytis grey mould. Monitor hot, dry foliage undersides for spider mites.

sections.title: Annual Phenology & Six-Season Rhythms
sections.subtitle: Flowering, fruiting, vegetative flush, and Shororitu synchrony
sections.summary: Seasonal cadence across Bengal's six-season cycle (Late Autumn (হেমন্ত), Winter (শীত)).
paragraphs: Marigold (Tagetes erecta) aligns its vegetative flushes, anthesis, and fruit maturation tightly with Bengal's Shororitu photoperiod and monsoon moisture transitions, showing peak biological activity during Late Autumn (হেমন্ত), Winter (শীত).

Late Autumn (হেমন্ত): Seedlings transplanted into raised nursery beds rapidly form dense bushy crowns rich in lutein-pigmented buds. Winter (শীত): Abundant golden-orange globular blossoms harvested across Gadkhali for winter garlands and cultural festivals.

sections.title: Seed Germination Biology & Propagation
sections.subtitle: Dormancy regulation, nursery media, and clonal propagation
sections.summary: Reproductive biology and reliable seed or vegetative propagation techniques for Marigold.
paragraphs: Marigold (Tagetes erecta) exhibits dual reproductive versatility through wind-, pollinator-, or gravity-dispersed seed cohorts alongside rapid vegetative renewal via herbaceous stem cuttings, rhizome splits, or nodal rooting. Mature seed capsules collected just prior to dehiscence retain strong vigor in dry shaded storage for moderate periods.
Rooting auxin pre-treatment on semi-ripe nodal cuttings during warm humid months accelerates adventitious root initiation within 10 to 21 days in porous coco-peat and vermicompost propagation trays.

subblocks.heading: Seed Germination
subblocks.text: Surface-sown or lightly covered in sterile porous mix; germinates in 7–21 days under ambient humidity.

subblocks.heading: Vegetative Method
subblocks.text: Two-node terminal cuttings or clump division rooted in misted, filtered-light benches.

sections.title: Pathology Defense, Vectors & Organic IPM
sections.subtitle: Phytoalexin resilience, fungal prophylaxis, and predator guilds
sections.summary: Biochemical defense mechanisms and low-impact organic IPM guidelines for Tagetes erecta.
paragraphs: In humid South Asian and tropical growing belts, Marigold (Tagetes erecta) relies on secondary terpenoid resins, foliar trichomes, and phytoalexin phenolics as front-line biochemical deterrence against herbivores and opportunistic pathogens. Prolonged monsoon waterlogging or stagnant canopy humidity can nonetheless encourage anthracnose (Colletotrichum spp.), powdery mildew, leaf-spot fungi, or root-zone Pythium.

Organic Integrated Pest Management (IPM) prioritizes preventive airflow pruning, Trichoderma-enriched compost amendments around feeder roots, and targeted cold-pressed Azadirachta indica (neem) oil sprays at dusk to suppress sap-sucking aphids, scale insects, and mealybugs without harming native pollinators.

subblocks.heading: Fungal Management
subblocks.text: Prevent overhead foliar wetness at dusk; maintain canopy aeration and copper/Trichoderma prophylaxis.

subblocks.heading: Organic Pest Control
subblocks.text: Neem kernel emulsion (3–5 ml/L) plus conservation of hoverfly and ladybird predator guilds.

sections.title: Conservation Standing & Climate Resilience
sections.subtitle: Population security, agroforestry corridors, and stress tolerance
sections.summary: Biogeographic conservation standing and climate adaptation traits of Marigold.
paragraphs: Across its native and naturalized distribution (Mexico & Central America), Marigold (Tagetes erecta) demonstrates strong ecological plasticity across alluvial floodplains, homestead agroforestry plots, and urban biodiversity corridors. While cultivated stands remain broadly secure, landrace genetic erosion, coastal salinity shifts, and wetland drainage threaten wild ecotypes and heritage regional varieties.

Long-term resilience depends on decentralized in-situ homestead stewardship, wetland buffer conservation, and botanical garden germplasm collections preserving drought-, flood-, and salinity-tolerant alleles amid shifting monsoon regimes.

subblocks.text: Adapted to Mexico & Central America thermal oscillations and seasonal hydrological extremes.

subblocks.text: Preserve traditional landraces, pollinator corridors, and living herbarium voucher plots.

sections.title: Horticultural Spacing, Pruning & Telemetry
sections.subtitle: Plot geometry, canopy shaping, and calibrated soil-climate meters
sections.summary: Calibrated horticultural parameters: pH 6.0 – 7.2 (Slightly acidic to neutral), Full Sun to Partial Filtered Light (6+ hrs), and structural spacing guidance.
paragraphs: Optimal managed cultivation of Marigold (Tagetes erecta) calibrates root-zone chemistry around pH 6.0 – 7.2 (Slightly acidic to neutral) inside well-drained organic sandy-clay loam. Providing adequate crown spacing prevents humidity buildup and lets lower shoots capture uniform irradiance across full sun to partial filtered light (6+ hrs).

Light corrective pruning immediately after main flowering or harvest periods redirects assimilates into healthy vegetative framework, while moisture scheduling (moderate deep watering scaled to monsoon rhythm) stabilizes root turgor without inducing hypoxia.

sections.title: Evolutionary Genetics & Adaptive Phylogeny
sections.subtitle: Asterales clade divergence and Asteraceae genomic traits
sections.summary: Phylogenetic placement of genus Tagetes within order Asterales (Eudicot (Asterids)).
paragraphs: Modern molecular phylogenetics (APG IV) places Tagetes erecta inside family Asteraceae (অ্যাস্টেরেসি (সূর্যমুখী গোত্র)), order Asterales, clade Eudicot (Asterids). Earth's largest flowering plant family, distinguished by composite flower heads (capitula) uniting sterile ray florets and fertile central disc florets.

Within genus Tagetes, specialized morphological adaptations—such as capitulum inflorescence mimicking a single giant blossom—reflect co-evolutionary specialization with regional pollinator guilds and abiotic habitat filters.

sections.title: Field Identification Key & Diagnostic Checks
sections.subtitle: Macro-morphological verification against look-alike taxa
sections.summary: Rapid field-sheet checklist for confirming Tagetes erecta (Gada (গাঁদা)).
paragraphs: Field verification of Marigold (Tagetes erecta) rests on recognizing key Asteraceae family markers: Capitulum inflorescence mimicking a single giant blossom; Single-seeded achene fruits frequently topped with calyx pappus; Rich carotenoid pigments and heliotropic or aromatic terpenes. Inspecting fresh leaf arrangement, stem surface texture, and reproductive architecture together eliminates confusion with sympatric congeners.
